lesson.title: Heads I Made It Happen, Tails It Wasn't My Fault
lesson.summary: Self-serving bias is the tendency to credit our successes to our own qualities while blaming our failures on outside circumstances, a pattern that helps protect self-esteem but can also distort how fairly we judge our own performance.
lesson.body:
Attribution theory gives us the internal versus external distinction, and self-serving bias describes a lopsided way people apply it to themselves. When something goes well, we tend to attribute it internally, to our own effort, skill, or intelligence, "I aced the exam because I really understand the material." When something goes poorly, we tend to attribute it externally, to bad luck, an unfair test, or circumstances beyond our control, "I failed because the professor grades unfairly and the questions were tricky." The same student, the same class, the same kind of outcome, but the direction of the explanation flips depending on whether the outcome was good or bad.

This pattern shows up across an enormous range of everyday contexts. Athletes and coaches tend to credit wins to skill and preparation while attributing losses to bad officiating, injuries, or an unlucky bounce. Drivers involved in accidents disproportionately describe the other driver or the road conditions as the cause. Employees who receive a strong performance review tend to see it as proof of their ability, while a poor review gets chalked up to an unreasonable boss or a bad year for the whole team. Dale Miller and Michael Ross reviewed a wide body of this evidence in a well known 1975 paper and concluded that, while not every finding fits perfectly, the overall pattern of self-serving attribution is real and shows up reliably enough to be treated as a genuine bias rather than a coincidence.

Two broad explanations are usually offered for why this bias exists. A motivational account says people are protecting their self-esteem and their public image, taking credit for success and deflecting blame for failure because that feels better and looks better to others. A more cognitive account points out that people genuinely do have different information available for successes versus failures. We usually intend to succeed and put in visible effort toward that goal, so when we succeed, the internal cause is easy to see, while the specific reasons behind a failure are often less visible to us in the moment, which can make external explanations feel more available and more plausible, not just more comfortable.

Self-serving bias is not universal or unlimited. Its size tends to vary with how much is riding on the outcome and with culture, and researchers have found it tends to be somewhat less pronounced in cultures that place less emphasis on individual achievement and more on group harmony, though it appears in some form quite broadly. It also connects directly to the two attribution biases already covered: it overlaps with actor-observer bias whenever the actor happens to be judging their own good or bad outcomes, and it sets up locus of control, discussed next, since a person's general habit of crediting or blaming themselves for outcomes is closely tied to whether they see control over their life as coming from within or from outside themselves.
